usage: Rising tone when you pick up an unknown call
여보세요 opens the line, 안녕하세요 is the real greeting
Re-used mid-call to check a silent line
Hello, is that the Korean restaurant?
Confirming you reached the right place
examples: 여보세요?
Hello?
The bare one-word answer when your phone rings
여보세요, 김민수 씨 휴대폰 맞으세요?
Hello, is this Kim Minsu's phone?
Everyday check that you got the right number
여보세요? 여보세요? 소리가 끊겨요.
Hello? Hello? You're cutting out.
Repeated when the line drops and you're reconnecting
nuance: 여보세요 is the dedicated telephone 'hello' and is almost never used face to face — saying it to someone in front of you sounds like a joke or a way to snap a daydreamer back to attention ('hello? anybody home?'). It comes from 여기 보세요 ('look here / over here'), literally a call for attention, which is why it also works mid-call to test a quiet line. The everyday in-person greeting is 안녕하세요, and the two are not interchangeable: 안녕하세요 means 'are you at peace', a wellbeing greeting, while 여보세요 just opens a voice channel. Register is neutral-polite (the 세요 ending), fine for strangers, customer service, and elders alike; the blunt 반말 version 여보 has drifted into meaning 'honey/darling' between spouses, so never shorten 여보세요 to 여보 with a stranger. The English-speaker trap is using it like 'hi' when you meet someone — keep it strictly for phones and for getting a distracted person's attention.

usage: Standard polite 'who's calling' on an unknown number
실례지만 softens a direct identity question
Who was that on the phone?
Past tense, asking a family member after they hang up
Might I ask who this is?
혹시 makes it tentative and extra gentle
examples: 여보세요? 누구세요?
Hello? Who's calling?
The basic pairing when you don't recognize the number
죄송하지만 누구세요? 잘 못 들었어요.
Sorry, who is this? I didn't catch it.
Everyday follow-up when a name was unclear
누구세요? 성함이 어떻게 되세요?
Who is this? May I have your name?
At a desk, asking a caller to identify themselves
nuance: 누구세요? is the polite way to ask a caller's identity, built from 누구 ('who') plus the honorific 이세요 — so literally it honors the unknown person while you find out who they are. The crucial contrast for learners is against 누구야? and 누구냐?: those are 반말/blunt and sound suspicious or hostile ('who the heck are you?'), fine only with close friends, never with a stranger on the line. For maximum politeness Koreans upgrade to 누구시죠? or 어디세요? (the latter literally 'where are you from?', i.e. which company/office), which is the norm in business calls. Note the particle trap: it stands alone, so don't bolt on 가/이 as in 누구가세요 — that's ungrammatical. Another pitfall is answering your own phone with 누구세요?; if you placed the call, you say who YOU are first (저는 ...예요), and 누구세요? is reserved for when you RECEIVE a call from someone unknown. Pair it naturally with a soft opener like 실례지만 or 죄송하지만 so it doesn't sound like an interrogation.

usage: 지금 ('now') pins it to this moment
Is it all right to talk?
괜찮으세요 lifts it to a more deferential level
Would later be okay to talk?
Offering to call back at a better time
examples: 여보세요, 지금 통화 괜찮아요?
Hello, is now a good time to talk?
The polite opener right after the greeting
혹시 바쁘세요? 잠깐 통화 괜찮아요?
Are you busy by chance? Got a moment to talk?
Everyday check before launching in
회의 중이세요? 그럼 끝나고 통화 괜찮으세요?
Are you in a meeting? Then is after it okay to talk?
Negotiating a better time at work
nuance: 통화 괜찮아요? literally asks 'is the phone-call okay?' — 통화 is Sino-Korean 通話 ('通 pass-through' + '話 talk'), i.e. a connected voice conversation, distinct from 전화 (電話 'electric-talk', the call/the phone as a device or the act of phoning). So you ask 통화 괜찮아요?, not 전화 괜찮아요?, because you're asking about the act of conversing, not the device. 괜찮아요 itself is the all-purpose 'it's fine / no problem', and here it means 'is it a convenient moment'. The near-synonym is 시간 괜찮아요? ('do you have time?'), which is broader and works for in-person meetings too, whereas 통화 괜찮아요? is specifically about taking THIS call right now. Register: the 요-ending is polite-casual and standard among colleagues and acquaintances; bump to 통화 괜찮으세요? for clients or elders. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'can you talk?' as 말할 수 있어요? — that asks about physical ability to speak and sounds odd; the idiomatic frame is the convenience check 통화 괜찮아요?.

usage: 잘 = 'well', so literally 'doesn't reach me well'
소리가 names the subject doing the not-reaching
It's choppy so I can't hear.
A bit louder please, I can't hear.
examples: 여보세요? 잘 안 들려요.
Hello? I can't hear you well.
First sign the line is bad
미안해요, 잘 안 들려요. 크게 말해 줄래요?
Sorry, I can't hear well. Could you speak up?
Everyday request for volume
여기 지하라서 신호가 약해요. 잘 안 들려요.
I'm in a basement so the signal's weak. I can't hear.
Explaining the cause on a dropping call
nuance: 잘 안 들려요 is built on 들리다, the INTRANSITIVE/potential 'to be heard / be audible' — not 듣다 'to listen'. This is the key learner trap: 듣다 is what YOU actively do (저는 음악을 들어요 'I listen to music'), while 들리다 is what the sound DOES on its own ('it reaches the ear'). So a bad line is 안 들려요 ('[your voice] isn't getting through'), never 안 들어요 (which would mean 'I'm not listening', implying you're ignoring them — rude on a call!). The 려 comes from the 리 of 들리- meeting the 어요 ending: 들리+어요 → 들려요. Add 잘 ('well') and the negative 안 and you get 'doesn't come through well'. A close cousin is 안 들렸어요 (past, 'I didn't catch that') versus the present 안 들려요 ('I can't hear you [ongoing]'). Phrase it with 소리가 (the sound as subject) or 신호가 약하다 ('the signal is weak') for natural collocation. Register: the 요-form is polite and perfectly normal with anyone; just don't clip it to 안 들려 with strangers.

usage: 걸다 = to place a call; 다시 = again
I'll call back in a bit.
I'll be the one to call back.
제가 stresses YOU will redial, not them
Let me hang up and call again.
Common fix for a glitchy connection
examples: 미안, 지금 바빠서 이따 다시 걸게요.
Sorry, I'm busy now so I'll call back later.
Politely postponing
소리가 자꾸 끊겨요. 끊고 다시 걸게요.
It keeps cutting out. I'll hang up and redial.
Fixing a bad line
회의 끝나고 30분 후에 다시 걸게요.
I'll call back 30 minutes after the meeting.
Giving a concrete time
nuance: 다시 걸게요 hinges on two things English speakers stumble over. First, the verb: Korean 'to make a phone call' is 전화를 걸다 — 걸다 literally 'to hang/hook', a relic of old hook-and-cradle phones — so you 'hook' a call, and 다시 걸다 = 'call again'. Don't use 부르다 ('to call out a name / summon'), which never means telephoning. Second, the ending -ㄹ게요 (걸+게요) is a SPEAKER'S PROMISE/INTENTION: it commits ME to the action and softly implies it's for your sake, unlike the plain future -ㄹ 거예요 ('I will [just a prediction]'). So 다시 걸게요 = 'I'll redial (you can count on me to)', warmer than 다시 걸 거예요. Crucially, -ㄹ게요 can only take a FIRST-PERSON subject — you can't say 그 사람이 다시 걸게요 about someone else. The natural opposite is 다시 걸어 주세요 ('please call me back'), which you say when THEY should redial. Pair with 이따 / 나중에 / 끊고 for timing. Register: polite-casual, fine for friends and coworkers; for a client use the deferential 다시 연락드리겠습니다.

Saying 다시 걸게요 when the OTHER person should redial — -ㄹ게요 promises that YOU will act; if they should call, it's 다시 걸어 주세요.
Confusing it with the flat prediction 다시 걸 거예요 — that just forecasts a fact; -ㄹ게요 makes it a personal commitment to the listener.

usage: 문자(를) 보내다 = to send a text
I'll send the address by text.
I'll check and then text you.
examples: 전화 안 받으면 문자 보낼게요.
If you don't pick up, I'll text you.
Backup plan if the call fails
시간하고 장소는 문자 보낼게요.
I'll text you the time and place.
Sending details to keep on record
지금 통화 어려우니까 문자 보낼게요.
It's hard to talk now, so I'll text instead.
Choosing text over a call
nuance: 문자 보낼게요 = 'I'll send a text'. 문자 is Sino-Korean 文字 ('文 writing' + '字 character'), so literally 'written characters' — short for 문자 메시지 (SMS). The big learner contrast is 문자 vs 카톡 vs 메시지: 문자 is specifically a phone SMS, 카톡 (KakaoTalk) is the messenger app most Koreans actually use day to day, and 메시지 is the generic 'message'; younger people often say 카톡 보낼게요 in real life. Don't confuse 문자 with 전화 (a call) — 문자 is text, 전화 is voice; mixing them changes what you promise to do. The verb is 보내다 ('to send'), and note the channel particle: 문자로 보내다 = 'send BY text', where 로 marks the means. The ending -ㄹ게요 again makes it a personal promise to the listener (first-person only, warmer than the bare future). A subtle trap: 보내 줄게요 (with 주다) adds a nuance of 'I'll send it FOR you / as a favor', slightly more considerate than plain 보낼게요. Collocations: 주소/시간/사진/링크를 문자로 보내다.

usage: Please leave your name and number.
Please leave it after the beep.
Please leave a brief message of your business.
examples: 지금 자리에 안 계세요. 메모 남겨 주세요.
He's not at his desk now. Please leave a message.
Reception relaying that someone's away
연결이 안 되네요. 메모 남겨 주시면 전해 드릴게요.
I can't reach them. If you leave a message I'll pass it on.
Offering to relay
삐 소리 후에 성함과 메모 남겨 주세요.
After the beep, please leave your name and message.
Full voicemail greeting
nuance: 메모 남겨 주세요 = 'please leave a message (for me to give them)'. 메모 is the loanword 'memo', here meaning a phone message/note; 남기다 is the TRANSITIVE 'to leave (something) behind, to make remain' — distinct from 떠나다 ('to leave / depart a place'). English 'leave a message' uses one word for both senses, so the trap is reaching for 떠나다: you'd never say 메시지를 떠나다 — a left-behind note is 남기다. The construction -아/어 주세요 ('please do X for me') makes it a polite request done as a favor; dropping 주세요 leaves the bare command 남겨 ('leave it!'), which sounds curt. Near-synonyms: 전할 말씀 있으세요? ('do you have something to relay?') is what a secretary asks, and 메시지 남겨 주세요 (with the English-derived 메시지) is interchangeable, slightly more modern. In office/voicemail register the whole phrase is polite-formal and very common. Collocations: 성함/연락처/용건을 남기다 ('leave your name/contact/business'). A finer point: 메모를 남기다 = leave a written note; 음성 메시지를 남기다 = leave a voice message.

Dropping 주세요 and saying just 메모 남겨 — that's a blunt command; the -어 주세요 frame makes it a polite request.
Calling the message 편지 — 편지 is a posted letter; a phone message is 메모 / 메시지.

usage: 전화를 끊다 = to hang up; -지 마세요 = don't
One sec, please don't hang up.
Buying a moment to check something
바로 바꿔 드릴 테니 끊지 마세요.
I'll transfer you right away, so don't hang up.
examples: 잠깐만요, 끊지 마세요. 확인해 볼게요.
One moment, don't hang up. Let me check.
Pausing to look something up
끊지 마세요, 담당자 바꿔 드릴게요.
Don't hang up, I'll put you through to the right person.
Transferring a call
아직 할 얘기가 남았어요. 끊지 마세요.
I still have things to say. Don't hang up.
Keeping a personal call going
nuance: 끊지 마세요 = 'please don't hang up'. The verb 끊다 means 'to cut / sever' and is exactly how Korean conceptualizes ending a call (전화를 끊다 = 'cut the phone'), the natural opposite of 걸다 ('hook/place a call'). The grammar to master is the negative command -지 말다 → -지 마세요 ('please don't ~'): you attach -지 마세요 to the dictionary stem, so 끊다 → 끊지 마세요. The classic learner error is mixing this up with 안: 안 끊어요 just states 'I'm not hanging up', it does NOT tell the other person to stop — prohibitions need -지 마세요, not 안. Politeness ladder: 끊지 마 (반말, only with close friends), 끊지 마세요 (polite, default), 끊지 마십시오 (formal announcements). Note 끊다 also covers 'quit/cut off' more broadly — 담배를 끊다 ('quit smoking'), 연락을 끊다 ('cut off contact') — so context tells you it's the phone. Collocates with 잠깐만요 ('just a sec') and 바꿔 드릴게요 ('I'll transfer you'), the two things most often said right before it.

usage: 잠깐 = a brief moment; 기다리다 = to wait
잠깐만 (with 만 'only') feels softer and shorter
-어 주세요 adds a favor nuance, gentler
여기서 marks the place to wait
examples: 잠깐 기다리세요. 자리에 안 계세요.
Please hold. He's not at his desk.
Reception checking availability
네, 잠깐만 기다리세요. 바로 바꿔 드릴게요.
Yes, one moment, I'll put you right through.
Before a transfer
잠깐 기다려 주세요. 메모 좀 찾을게요.
Please wait a sec, let me find the note.
Searching for something mid-call
nuance: 잠깐 기다리세요 = 'please wait a moment'. 잠깐 is an adverb meaning 'briefly, for a short while' — its near-twin 잠시 means the same but is a touch more formal/written (잠시만 기다려 주십시오 is the announcement-style version you hear at counters), while 잠깐 is the everyday spoken choice. The verb 기다리다 'to wait' is a 르-irregular only in some forms but regular here (기다리+세요). The honorific request ending -(으)세요 makes it a polite instruction. A key nuance for learners: 잠깐 기다리세요 (-세요) is a polite COMMAND, whereas 잠깐 기다려 주세요 (-어 주세요) frames it as a favor and sounds warmer/more considerate — in service settings the 주세요 version is preferred for customers. Don't confuse 기다리다 ('wait') with 기대하다 ('to expect/look forward to') — similar opening syllable, totally different meaning. Also avoid the English calque 'hold on' as 잡으세요 (잡다 = physically grab); Korean 'hold the line' is simply 기다리세요 or 끊지 마세요. Collocates with 잠깐만요 ('just a sec!'), the interjection Koreans throw out to freeze the moment.

usage: Please contact me when you arrive.
Please be sure to reach out.
examples: 시간 되면 연락해 주세요.
Get in touch when you have time.
Casual-polite open invitation
결정하시면 저한테 연락해 주세요.
Once you decide, please contact me.
저한테 marks 'to me' as the destination
문제 생기면 언제든지 연락해 주세요.
If any problem comes up, contact me anytime.
Reassuring availability
nuance: 연락해 주세요 = 'please contact me'. 연락 is Sino-Korean 連絡 ('連 connect/link' + '絡 entwine/tie'), literally 'making a link', so it covers ALL channels — call, text, email, messenger — and is broader than 전화하다 ('to phone specifically'). That breadth is the point: when you don't care HOW they reach you, 연락하다 is the word. The verb is a 하다-verb (연락 + 하다 → 연락해요), and 연락해 주세요 = 연락해 + 주세요 ('do the contacting for me'), a polite favor request. Watch the destination particle: 'contact ME' is 저한테/저에게 연락해 주세요, not 저를 — 연락하다 takes 한테/에게 (the 'to' marker), so 저를 연락하다 is wrong. Register: this 주세요 form is polite-standard for peers and most situations; to a client or superior, upgrade to the humble 연락 주시면 감사하겠습니다 or 연락 부탁드립니다. Note the very common clipped collocation 연락 주세요 (dropping 하), which natives say constantly and means the same. Don't confuse 연락 with 약속 ('a promised appointment') — 연락 is just reaching out, no commitment to meet.

usage: [name] 바꿔 주세요 = ask for that person
Could you put the person in charge on?
If the manager's there, please put him on.
Asking a switchboard for an extension
examples: 여보세요, 박 과장님 바꿔 주세요.
Hello, please put Manager Park on.
Standard office request
엄마 집에 계시면 바꿔 주세요.
If mom's home, please put her on.
Calling a family landline
죄송하지만 책임자 바꿔 주시겠어요?
Sorry, could you put the supervisor on?
Extra-polite -시겠어요 version
nuance: 바꿔 주세요 on the phone means 'please switch the call over to ___ / put them on'. The verb 바꾸다 'to change, switch, swap' is the same word used for exchanging goods (옷을 바꾸다 'exchange clothes') — and THAT overlap is the trap: on a call, 바꿔 주세요 isn't asking to trade anything, it's asking the answerer to hand the receiver to someone else, i.e. swap who's speaking. So 김 선생님 바꿔 주세요 = 'change [the speaker] to Mr. Kim', not 'exchange Mr. Kim'. Form: 바꾸+어 주세요 → 바꿔 주세요 (the ㅜ+어 contracts to 워), with -어 주세요 making it a polite favor. The pattern is simply [person/extension] + 바꿔 주세요. A near-synonym in formal/business contexts is 연결해 주세요 ('please connect me'), which a switchboard operator expects; 바꿔 주세요 is what you say when a human picked up and you want a different person. Don't reach for the English calque 'put on' literally — there's no 놓다/올리다 here; the idiom is 바꾸다. For extra courtesy, 바꿔 주시겠어요? ('would you put them on?') is softer than the plain request.

usage: 거셨어요 = honorific, telling the CALLER they erred
examples: 죄송합니다, 전화 잘못 걸었어요.
I'm sorry, I dialed the wrong number.
Polite apology before hanging up
어, 전화 잘못 걸었어요. 끊을게요.
Oh, wrong number. I'll hang up.
Realizing and bowing out fast
번호를 잘못 봐서 전화 잘못 걸었어요.
I misread the number, so I dialed wrong.
Explaining the slip
nuance: 전화 잘못 걸었어요 = 'I called the wrong number'. The load-bearing word is 잘못, an ADVERB meaning 'mistakenly, wrongly' — and learners must not confuse it with the NOUN 잘못 ('a fault/wrongdoing', as in 제 잘못이에요 'it's my fault'). As an adverb it sits right before the verb: 잘못 걸다 ('dial wrongly'), 잘못 보다 ('misread'), 잘못 듣다 ('mishear'). Don't fuse it as 잘못걸다 — keep 잘못 as a separate word modifying the verb. The verb 걸다 here is the same 'place a call' (전화를 걸다); the past 걸었어요 comes from 걸+었어요. A frequent mix-up is 잘못 vs 못: 못 걸었어요 means 'I COULDN'T place the call' (inability), while 잘못 걸었어요 means 'I placed it WRONGLY' (wrong number) — totally different, so the spacing and word choice matter. Etiquette/register: Koreans almost always lead with 죄송해요/죄송합니다 and a quick 끊을게요 ('I'll hang up') rather than just silently dropping; the 요-ending here is polite and appropriate to a stranger you've accidentally dialed. If you RECEIVE such a call, you tell them 전화 잘못 거셨어요 (honorific, 'you've dialed wrong').
